A policy adopted through legitimate, accountable processes carries real weight precisely because it reflects a shared framework in which no one gets to unilaterally impose their will. But the teacher's professional judgment also matters—she has standing, and if she sees genuine harm to students (who themselves have equal standing), silently defying the rule isn't the ideal expression of that. The concern is that quiet unilateral defiance, however well-intentioned, substitutes her private judgment for collective authority. In a society of equals, the better path is to voice objection, contest the policy openly, and seek to change it—not simply act as if her view overrides everyone else's. Yet the students' equal standing and vulnerability give her objection real moral force, so the rule doesn't automatically win.
